card.law_is_about: Creating a regulated adult cannabis market.
card.they_want: Oppose adult liberalisation on youth-protection grounds.
card.they_claim: Cannabis accounts for over 30% of all inpatient addiction diagnoses.
card.the_problem: The cited share excludes alcohol and concerns a selected treatment dataset.

claim_quote.translation_en: Translation: more than 30% of all addiction-related diagnoses

locator.section: 3.2. Gesundheitliche Folgen einer Legalisierung von Cannabisprodukten

supplementary_locator.note: Exact 33.5% appears here; page 15 uses rounded 33%.

counter_quote.translation_en: Translation: excluding alcohol as the principal diagnosis

correction: The cited 33.5% describes selected nonalcohol drug principal diagnoses in DSHS services, not all addiction-related diagnoses. The original DSHS annual report separately reports cannabis as 9.2% of its broader inpatient principal-diagnosis distribution, based on completed treatments; that is contextual corroboration, not a national inpatient rate or a recalculation from the REITOX totals.
effect: Presenting the restricted share as an all-addiction share overstates its scope and strengthens the submission’s health-risk rationale.
direction_explanation: A larger apparent addiction-treatment share supports the author’s caution against adult liberalisation. This does not establish intent.
limits: The restricted 33.5% figure is valid. DSHS is a selected treatment-service sample, not the national hospital population. The annual report’s 9.2% concerns principal diagnoses among completed treatments in its specified sample and is not a corrected national rate. Total treatment volume and completed-treatment analytic bases must not be mixed. The adjacent hospital-treatment count belongs to another dataset. Cannabis-related harm and treatment demand remain real; no policy conclusion follows automatically. The finding concerns the scope of the cited figure; no national proportion or share including all secondary diagnoses is determined.
context_and_alternatives: The source chapter concerns illegal-drug treatment, which may explain the omitted qualification; the submission itself says all addiction-related diagnoses.

The report distinguishes DSHS specialised services from hospital-diagnosis statistics and rehabilitation. The adjacent 17,148 hospital cases are a different dataset and cannot be used as the numerator for the 33.5%.

A fresh read of the full eight-page submission found no explicit qualification limiting this sentence to the selected nonalcohol drug categories. Its wider cannabis focus could explain an implicit narrower meaning, but does not reproduce the source restriction. The health-risk rationale supports broader precautionary opposition; this statistic does not directly establish the asserted youth-protection effect.

The original DSHS annual report distinguishes total treatment volume from the completed-treatment group used for diagnosis analyses (methods page 5; treatment volume page 8; figure 4 page 11; table B page 54). Table B reports 3,897 cannabis principal diagnoses among 42,306 diagnoses in 210 facilities, with 0.3% unknown. This differs from simply multiplying the REITOX restricted share by its case totals, so the earlier approximate derived comparison has been withdrawn.

supplementary_evidence.paraphrase: Cannabis 9.2% (3,897 of 42,306 principal diagnoses); alcohol 68.6%; 210 facilities, 0.3% unknown; completed-treatment group. Figure 4 on page 11 presents the same shares.
supplementary_evidence.role: Contextual corroboration with a separately specified analytic base; not a national rate or substitute arithmetic for the REITOX percentage.

materiality_explanation: Major: removing the alcohol exclusion substantially broadens the represented burden. In the original DSHS report, alcohol accounts for 68.6% and cannabis for 9.2% of the broader principal-diagnosis distribution; the restricted 33.5% cannot be presented as the all-addiction share. This editorial materiality judgment is separate from direction and policy merits.

card.law_is_about: Creating a regulated adult cannabis market.
card.they_want: Oppose adult liberalisation on youth-protection grounds.
card.they_claim: Colorado traffic deaths caused by marijuana rose 32%.
card.the_problem: The matched statistic counts deaths in crashes involving a marijuana-positive operator; it does not establish causation.

claim_quote.translation_en: Translation: traffic deaths caused by marijuana by 32%

counter_quote.original: any time marijuana shows up in the toxicology report

correction: The matching 32% and 10%/19.26% figures in RMHIDTA concern marijuana-related traffic fatalities involving operators with positive tests, including combinations with alcohol or other drugs. Positive toxicology does not identify marijuana-caused deaths.
effect: Removes a claimed causal quantification from the traffic-safety argument.
direction_explanation: A quantified causal harm supports the author’s precautionary opposition. The road-safety discussion also supports greater traffic monitoring; no intent is inferred.
limits: This finding concerns the description of the strongly matched statistic, conditional on that source identification. The actual change in deaths causally attributable to cannabis is not established here and could coincidentally have been 32%; the toxicology series does not decide that question. Cannabis can impair driving, and legalisation may have traffic effects. The preceding CaPRis risk association remains a separate argument and is not disproved.
context_and_alternatives: The submission does not cite the traffic statistic locally; source identification is a strong matching inference from the exact 32% and 10%/~20% combination and its earlier citation of the 2015 RMHIDTA report.
RMHIDTA distinguishes DUID enforcement data from fatality toxicology data; its DUID discussion cannot supply causation for the separate fatality series.
The source says the 32% change is 2013–2014. Retail stores opened 1 January 2014; the submission’s 2013 sales reference is a separate chronological imprecision, not necessary to this finding.

A fresh full-context check considered the report’s neighbouring DUID causation language. That language concerns a different enforcement dataset and cannot supply causal attribution for the matched fatality series. The Colorado 2016 driver series is used only for a methodological warning, not as a replacement for the RMHIDTA operator series.

RMHIDTA also reports that 47% of operators in fatal crashes were tested in 2014 (physical page 24), and labels its 2014 FARS data preliminary when published (physical page 25). These reporting limits are preserved as context; they do not establish a different actual causal increase.

materiality_explanation: Major: the wording turns a toxicology association into an attributed cause of death, materially strengthening the evidence presented for the road-safety objection.

locator.paragraph: first sentence: which Annex 2 data can be exempted from transmission on confidentiality grounds

counter_quote.translation_en: Translation of fragment: Information is exempt from the publication obligation

supplementary_counter_quote.translation_en: Translation of fragment: no exception for information

locator.paragraph: third: expressly concerns transmission to the federal authority, including confidential information

correction: The amendment inserts an exception only from publication in §13(1). The retained first sentence separately requires transmission to the federal authority; the draft also adds IT-operator cooperation and §13(3) federal transmission to the European database with confidential handling. Its explanatory memorandum expressly says there is no confidentiality exception from transmission. The described permission to withhold the register data is therefore not in this exact draft. The requested list would introduce specified transmission exemptions where this draft provides none, rather than merely narrow an existing broad transmission exemption.
effect: Removes the factual premise that this amendment permits wholesale non-reporting and makes EU reporting impossible. That premise directly supports the requested exhaustive list and extra justification requirement.
limits: This is a mismatch about the scope of the proposed reporting exception, not a prediction that all firms will comply. Confidentiality can restrict what the public, municipalities or researchers can see; those separate access concerns are not refuted. The author may prefer more public transparency or tighter enforcement. The finding does not establish complete reporting, accurate data, adequate enforcement, appropriate confidentiality boundaries or the merits of the proposed list. No intent is inferred.
direction_explanation: True: conflating public publication with confidential regulatory transmission makes the requested exhaustive list and additional justification duty appear necessary to keep the register complete.
context_checks: Read all ten pages, particularly the full finding, request, proposed list and rationale on pages 7–8; visually inspected both pages.

Tested the public-facing-register reading. The author expressly discusses inability to report to the EU, asks for exemptions from transmission to be enumerated, and says the information is sent only to an authority. Those contextual statements make this more than a complaint about loss of public access.

Checked the complete amendment on draft page 15 together with explanation page 66. Existing § 13(1) separates publication and transmission; did not mistake confidentiality of regulatory holdings for permission not to submit them.
The author correctly identifies several other changes and bracketed 80% design-PUE option in this consultation version; the critique is not judged against a later June cabinet draft.
Other DCE comments about grandfathering, technical feasibility, certification or foreseeable behaviour are not adjudicated in this finding.

card.law_is_about: A pending revision of German energy-efficiency duties and implementation of the EU Energy Efficiency Directive.
card.they_want: Delete or weaken the national energy-efficiency targets in § 4 EnEfG.
card.they_claim: Germany used about 3,273 TWh of final energy in 2020; reducing it 11.7% gives an EU-consistent 2030 level around 2,890 TWh, making the German 1,867 TWh target excessively strict.
card.the_problem: The 2020 quantity is primary energy, not final energy. The 11.7% EU target also uses modelled 2030 consumption from the 2020 reference scenario, not observed pandemic-year consumption. The derived comparison is invalid.

claim_quote.original: Der Deutsche Endenergieverbrauch lag 2020 bei 402 Mio. t. SKE, bzw. rund 3272.682 TWh.
claim_quote.translation_en: Translation: German final energy consumption in 2020 was 402 million tonnes of coal equivalent, or about 3,272.682 TWh.

request_quote.translation_en: Translation of request fragment: This section should be deleted without replacement
request_quote.context: The complete sentence alternatively asks for weakening to EED requirements. Both alternatives are grounded in the same comparison.

counter_quote.original: Der Primärenergieverbrauch in Deutschland betrug im Jahr 2020 insgesamt 11.784 PJ oder 402,1 Mio. t SKE
counter_quote.translation_en: Translation: Primary energy consumption in Germany in 2020 totalled 11,784 PJ or 402.1 million tonnes of coal equivalent

baseline_counter_quote.original: compared to the 2020 projections for energy use in 2030

correction: The approximately 402 million-tonne figure matches the statistics producer's 2020 primary-energy total, whose 2021 report gives 402.1 million tonnes/11,784 PJ. Its final-energy infographic instead gives 8,341 PJ, about 2,317 TWh. Category definitions and subsequent revisions may change the precise final figure, not convert the primary total into final energy. Separately, EED Article 4 and recital 28 apply 11.7% to modelled 2030 use in the 2020 reference scenario at EU level. National indicative contributions must account for the directive's criteria; multiplying observed German 2020 use by 0.883 does not produce Germany's EU minimum.
effect: Removes the numerical basis for claiming a 2,890 TWh EU comparator against the 1,867 TWh German target. The primary/final mislabelling inflates the starting final-energy quantity by roughly 40%, while the reference-year substitution independently prevents the calculation from establishing the asserted EU comparator.
limits: This does not prove the German target is feasible, economically optimal or legally mandatory at exactly 1,867 TWh. It does not establish motive. The statement correctly mentions the 2020 reference scenario on page 2; the error arises when the next page substitutes a pandemic-year consumption figure. Simply replacing the starting quantity with actual 2020 final energy and multiplying 0.883 would still not calculate the correct EU-based national contribution. The EED contains a binding collective final-energy target, an indicative primary-energy target and national indicative contributions; do not portray the 11.7% as an identical binding reduction imposed on every state.

card.they_want: Oppose acceleration on the stated ground that technical and economic prerequisites are missing.
card.they_claim: No industrial gas turbine anywhere had operated on pure hydrogen.
card.the_problem: An industrial SGT-400 turbine had run on 100% hydrogen in France in 2023.

counter_quote.original: gespeichert und zum Betrieb einer Siemens Energy SGT-400 Industriegasturbine verwendet.
counter_quote.translation_en: Translation: stored and used to operate a Siemens Energy SGT-400 industrial gas turbine.

locator.paragraph: First body paragraph; same paragraph identifies 100% renewable hydrogen

correction: The 13 October 2023 Siemens Energy/ENGIE/Centrax report describes operation of an industrial SGT-400 turbine at the Smurfit Kappa site in Saillat-sur-Vienne, France, on 100% renewable hydrogen. A separate NEDO primary report records 100%-hydrogen turbine heat-and-power delivery in Kobe in April 2018.
effect: Contradicts the categorical claim of zero prior industrial-turbine operation, weakening the stated technical-prerequisites argument against acceleration.
limits: An implicit reading of industrial as routine commercial or market-ready utility operation is possible. The counterexamples were demonstrations or verification tests; they do not establish routine commercial deployment, economics, utility-scale operation or readiness of the substantially larger Leipzig project. The actual sentence gives no commercial-maturity qualification, and the preceding sentence discusses a missing test run. The correction concerns categorical absence of prior operation only. It does not establish affordable hydrogen power or resolve hydrogen supply, safety or scaling. The cited article concerns Leipzig’s SGT-800 model; this finding does not contradict its model-specific account by substituting the different SGT-400.

additional_corroboration: European Commission CORDIS project record, 10 November 2023, explicitly describes actual 100% hydrogen operation of the SGT-400 industrial turbine. It also states that scaling and commercialisation remain further work; the demonstration/routine-operation limit is therefore preserved. Archived source id cordis-hyflexpower-2023.
context_and_alternatives: Read the 26 March 2024 Correctiv article expressly cited in footnote 9. Its no-prior-operation statement is explicitly limited to the SGT-800 turbines used in Leipzig, rather than all industrial turbine models. This strengthens a possible implicit model/utility context, which is preserved as an alternative. The submission’s following standalone sentence expands to worldwide industrial turbines without that qualification. Correctiv is used only to check the cited context; manufacturer, NEDO and Commission project records supply the counterevidence.

draft.document_date: 2024-09-20 committee cover; attached statement dated September 2024
draft.version_check: The 2024 bill, not the later 2025/2026 reintroduced bill, is the relevant version. The historical turbine assertion is independent of subsequent changes to the bill.

materiality_explanation: Major: the statement asserts complete worldwide absence of a key technical demonstration and uses this in the section arguing that the bill lacks technical prerequisites. Economic and permitting questions remain independent.
direction_explanation: The categorical absence claim reinforces opposition to accelerating hydrogen infrastructure. Demonstrated prior operation weakens that premise, without establishing that acceleration is desirable.
